overview.summary: Criminology studies crime, offenders, victims, and societal responses. This module summarizes foundational theories and modern perspectives.
learning_outcomes: Explain major criminological theories and what they attempt to predict/explain
Identify common misuse risks: overgeneralization, confirmation bias, and false causality

sections.title: Classical School
sections.one_liner: Crime as rational choice; deterrence through certainty/swiftness/proportionality.
core_ideas: Individuals have agency; decisions respond to incentives
Deterrence emphasizes certainty of consequence over severity
Proportionality: punishment should match harm/culpability

key_figures.name: Cesare Beccaria
key_figures.contrib: Proportional punishment, legality, due process ideals

common_misreadings: Assuming all offenders weigh costs rationally in the same way
where_it_helps: Policy: improving certainty of detection, reducing opportunity
Situational prevention: lighting, guardianship, design choices

sections.title: Positivist / Early Scientific Criminology
sections.one_liner: Crime as influenced by measurable individual and environmental factors.
core_ideas: Empirical observation and pattern-finding
Multiple interacting factors: biological, psychological, social
Risk-factor frameworks (not destiny): probabilities, not certainties
notes: Modern criminology rejects deterministic and discriminatory historical claims; focuses on ethical, validated research and contextual factors.
where_it_helps: Risk assessment frameworks (with strict fairness checks)

sections.title: Strain / Anomie
sections.one_liner: Crime can emerge when goals are blocked and pressure increases.
core_ideas: Discrepancy between cultural goals and legitimate means
Adaptive responses: innovation, retreatism, rebellion, ritualism
Stressors may be economic, relational, institutional

sections.title: Social Learning / Differential Association
sections.one_liner: Behavior is learned through peers, reinforcement, and modeling.
core_ideas: Definitions favorable/unfavorable to law are learned
Reinforcement strengthens behaviors
Networks shape opportunity and norms

sections.title: Control Theories
sections.one_liner: Most people avoid crime due to bonds and stakes in conformity.
core_ideas: Attachment, commitment, involvement, belief
Self-control: impulsivity can elevate risk in certain contexts
Prevention via strengthening bonds and structured opportunities
analysis_prompts: What stable routines reduce risk exposure?

sections.title: Routine Activity / Opportunity
sections.one_liner: Crime requires convergence of motivated offender, suitable target, and lack of guardianship.
core_ideas: Opportunity structures matter
Environmental design can reduce risk
Temporal/spatial patterns are critical

sections.title: Labeling / Social Reaction
sections.one_liner: Societal responses and stigma can shape future behavior.
core_ideas: Secondary deviance: identity effects
Discretion and inequality in processing
Policy focus: reintegration, reduce harmful stigma
quality_checks: Avoid assuming 'label' explains initial behavior; it explains pathways after system contact.

sections.title: Critical / Conflict Perspectives
sections.one_liner: Power, inequality, and enforcement priorities shape crime definitions and outcomes.
core_ideas: Law can reflect power structures
Enforcement is selective; outcomes vary by resources
Macro-level analysis of institutions and incentives
analysis_prompts: What incentives exist for enforcement focus?
How do resources and access affect outcomes?

sections.title: Victimology (Basics)
sections.one_liner: Victimization patterns and prevention without blame.
core_ideas: Risk is shaped by exposure, context, and guardianship
Trauma-informed approaches are essential
Never imply victim responsibility
